title: Chandni Chowk, 1675
hookLine: Guru Tegh Bahadur is beheaded in Delhi for defending others' freedom to practice their faith

lines: A PACKED STREET IN OLD DELHI.
cards: Chandni Chowk, Old Delhi, on an ordinary afternoon. The street is packed: rickshaws, spice sellers, wedding shops, sweet shops, horns, a river of people.
In the middle of it all stands a gurdwara with a gold dome, Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib. Sis means head. People step in off the noise, cover their heads, and go quiet.
They are standing on the spot where, in November 1675, a Guru was put to death, not for his own community, but for someone else's.

teach.b: The name Chandni Chowk is usually explained as the moonlit square. In 1675 it was the grand market street of the Mughal capital.
Tradition says that Guru Tegh Bahadur, held in Delhi, was given the same choice as his companions: accept Islam, or show a miracle to prove his standing, or die.
He refused all three. He would not give up his faith, and he would not perform wonders on demand. And so, in the open square, in November 1675, the ninth Guru was beheaded.
Remember why he had come. The pandits of Kashmir were Hindus. They wore the sacred thread and the forehead mark, which the Gurus had not taken up.
The Guru did not share their practices. He gave his life for their right to keep them. His son, who became the tenth Guru, later wrote about his father's death in a poem called Bachitar Natak.

teach.h: HE GAVE HIS HEAD, NOT HIS FAITH.
teach.b: In plain words, he says his father protected their forehead mark and their sacred thread, and did a great deed in this dark age; that he gave his head, but not his faith.
Because of this, Sikhs gave Guru Tegh Bahadur a title: Hind di chadar, the shield of India, the sheet that covered and protected people.
It is one thing to die for your own faith. It is something else to die so that people who believe differently from you may believe freely. That is what Sikhs remember in the square every year.

how: Sikhs mark Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom each year with prayers, processions and recitation, and many visit Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib in Chandni Chowk, Delhi, where he was beheaded.

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: his son's poem about his death

games.q: you're the Guru. you're told: convert, or show a miracle, or die. what do you do?
o: show a miracle and go free.
convert in name and keep your faith in secret.
games.why: he refused all three, and was beheaded in the square, giving his head, as his son wrote, but not his faith.

practice: Think of people, somewhere in the world, who aren't free to practice their faith or live by their conscience; they may believe very differently from you. Hold them in mind without needing to agree with them.
If you pray, you can pray for their freedom in whatever words are yours; if you don't, just wish it for them, sincerely, breath by breath.

wordCard.voice: Chandni Chowk. The moonlit square in Old Delhi where Guru Tegh Bahadur was beheaded in 1675, defending others' freedom to practice their faith.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: the sheet, or shield, of India, a title Sikhs give Guru Tegh Bahadur.

carryVoice: Your line: for another's faith. He gave his head, but not his faith. That's day seventy-nine.
